title: A Brief History of AI in Education
author: Philippa Hardman
summary: Philippa Hardman counters the sense that AI in education is new by pointing out that AI in Education (AIED) has existed for over 60 years. She gives a basic definition of AI as machines trained to recognise patterns, then walks through three established use cases: automated essay grading, personalised learning paths and intelligent tutoring systems. For each she names real examples such as Gradescope and E-rater, Carnegie Mellon's OpenSimon and Georgia Tech's Jill Watson. After each she adds a prediction, and all three converge on the same claim that the educator's role will shift away from grading and delivery toward data analysis, coaching and building and validating algorithms. The piece is an accessible overview with a hopeful tone and little critical scrutiny of efficacy or risk, so its value lies in the historical framing and the examples.
points: AIED predates ChatGPT by decades, so current excitement should be set against 60 years of machine learning applied to education.

Automated essay grading tools such as Gradescope and E-rater score on features like vocabulary, referencing and structure, and the author expects them to move toward judging critical thinking and originality.
Personalised learning tools like OpenSimon combine performance and behaviour data to predict which activities help each student, with future versions generating interventions on the fly.
Intelligent tutoring systems like Jill Watson offer both academic and social-emotional support, including a separate social agent that connects students to one another.
Hardman predicts the educator's role will shift toward teaching craft, data analysis and coaching, and eventually building and validating learning algorithms.
quotes: In fact, Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) has been around for over 60 years. We’ve been building AI-powered education technologies to design and deliver learning experiences for the same amount of time as we have explored space and researched nuclear physics and DNA.

Machine learning algorithms can be used to automatically score essays and written assignments, based on factors such as grammar, organisation, and coherence. This can save teachers time and provide students with more immediate feedback.
There is perhaps a not too distant future where a large part of the educator’s role is focused less on the admin of grading and more on the art and science of teaching, learning and research.

OpenSimon analyses student data and provides real-time personalised feedback based both student performance (e.g. how well they perform on a knowledge check) and student behaviour (e.g. how long they spend on certain activities).

One key benefit of intelligent tutoring systems like Jill Watson is that they can provide personalised support and feedback to each individual student, even in large classes where it may be difficult for the instructor to provide individual attention to each student.

Georgia Tech have recently created “Agent Smith” which will enable any academic to create their own version of Jill based on their own source materials. There is perhaps a not too distant future where a large part of the educator’s role is to understand and be able to build and validate machine learning algorithms to optimise their teaching impact at scale.
